## Problem 1

```{r}
# Set birthday function
birthday_sim = function(n) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  any(duplicated(birthdays))
}
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Simulate birthdays and check whether at least two people share a birthday
birthday_sim(10)
birthday_sim(23)
birthday_sim(50)
```

```{r}
set.seed(123)

# Estimate the probability for each group size using 10,000 simulations
birthday_results = 
  tibble(group_size = 2:50) |>
  mutate(
    probability = map_dbl(
      group_size,
      \(n) mean(replicate(10000, birthday_sim(n)))
    )
  )

birthday_results
```

```{r birthday_plot}
# Plot the estimated probability of a shared birthday by group size
birthday_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = probability)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +

  # Add a reference line at 50% probability
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0.5,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray50"
  ) +

  # Customize labels and axis scales
  labs(
    title = "Probability of a Shared Birthday by Group Size",
    x = "Group Size",
    y = "Probability of Shared Birthday"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 50, 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The simulation results show that the probability of at least two people sharing a birthday increases as group size increases. With 10 people, the estimated probability is `r scales::percent(birthday_results |> filter(group_size == 10) |> pull(probability), accuracy = 0.01)`, while with 23 people, it reaches `r scales::percent(birthday_results |> filter(group_size == 23) |> pull(probability), accuracy = 0.01)`, exceeding 50% despite the relatively small group size. As the group size increases further, the probability rises to `r scales::percent(birthday_results |> filter(group_size == 30) |> pull(probability), accuracy = 0.01)` for 30 people and `r scales::percent(birthday_results |> filter(group_size == 50) |> pull(probability), accuracy = 0.01)` for 50 people. These findings illustrate the birthday paradox, demonstrating that shared birthdays become likely even in moderately sized groups.



## Problem 2

```{r}
# List all CSV files in the data directory
file_names = list.files(
  path = "data",
  pattern = "\\.csv$",
  full.names = TRUE
)

# Check the number of files and inspect their names
length(file_names)
head(file_names)
```

```{r}
# Inspect the structure of an individual participant's data
example_subject = read_csv(file_names[1], show_col_types = FALSE)

glimpse(example_subject)
head(example_subject)
```

```{r}
# Create a dataframe of file names and read each participant's data
longitudinal_files =
  tibble(file_name = file_names) |>
  mutate(
    subject_data = map(
      file_name,
      \(file) read_csv(file, show_col_types = FALSE)
    )
  )

# Inspect the resulting dataframe and list-column
glimpse(longitudinal_files)
```

```{r}
# Extract subject IDs and treatment arms from file names
longitudinal_data =
  longitudinal_files |>
  mutate(
    file_id = basename(file_name),
    arm = case_when(
      str_starts(file_id, "con") ~ "Control",
      str_starts(file_id, "exp") ~ "Experimental"
    ),
    subject_id = str_extract(file_id, "\\d+")
  ) |>

  # Expand the participant data stored in the list-column
  unnest(subject_data) |>

  # Convert weekly observations from wide to long format
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    week = as.integer(str_remove(week, "week_")),
    arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Control", "Experimental"))
  ) |>

  # Keep only the variables needed for analysis
  select(subject_id, arm, week, observation) |>
  arrange(arm, subject_id, week)

# Check the dimensions and structure of the tidy dataset
dim(longitudinal_data)
glimpse(longitudinal_data)
head(longitudinal_data)
```

```{r spaghetti_plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
# Plot individual trajectories over time for each treatment arm
longitudinal_data |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = week,
      y = observation,
      group = subject_id
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(color = subject_id),
    linewidth = 0.7,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = subject_id),
    size = 1.5
  ) +

  # Display control and experimental groups separately
  facet_wrap(~ arm) +

  # Customize labels and plot appearance
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(
    title = "Individual Trajectories Over Time by Treatment Arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Subject ID"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

The spaghetti plot shows distinct longitudinal patterns between the control and experimental groups. In the control group, observations fluctuate over the eight weeks without a clear overall increasing or decreasing trend. In contrast, most subjects in the experimental group exhibit an upward trajectory, with observations generally increasing over time. By the later weeks, observations in the experimental group tend to be higher than those in the control group. Although individual variability is present in both groups, the experimental group demonstrates a more pronounced positive trend, suggesting a possible effect of the experimental intervention.


## Problem 3

```{r}
# Simulate one dataset and perform a one-sample t-test
sim_t_test = function(mu, n = 30, sigma = 5) {

  # Generate observations from a normal distribution
  sample_data = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

  # Test the null hypothesis that the population mean is zero
  test_result = t.test(sample_data, mu = 0)

  # Extract the estimated mean and p-value
  broom::tidy(test_result) |>
    select(estimate, p.value)
}
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Verify that the simulation function returns the expected variables
set.seed(123)

sim_t_test(mu = 0)
sim_t_test(mu = 3)
sim_t_test(mu = 6)
```

```{r}
# Set a random seed to ensure reproducible simulation results
set.seed(123)

# Run 5,000 simulations for each true population mean
simulation_results =
  tibble(true_mu = 0:6) |>
  mutate(
    simulation = map(
      true_mu,
      \(mu) map_dfr(
        1:5000,
        \(i) sim_t_test(mu = mu)
      )
    )
  ) |>

  # Combine all simulation results into a single dataframe
  unnest(simulation) |>
  mutate(
    reject_null = p.value < 0.05
  )

# Inspect the simulation results
dim(simulation_results)
glimpse(simulation_results)
head(simulation_results)
```

```{r}
# Calculate the estimated statistical power for each true mean
power_summary =
  simulation_results |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    n_simulations = n(),
    n_rejected = sum(reject_null),
    power = mean(reject_null),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Display the estimated power for each true mean
power_summary
```

```{r power_plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
# Plot statistical power against the true population mean
power_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = power)) +
  geom_line(
    color = "steelblue",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "steelblue",
    size = 2.5
  ) +

  # Add reference lines for the significance level and 80% power
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0.05,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray50"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0.80,
    linetype = "dotted",
    color = "darkgreen"
  ) +

  # Customize labels, scales, and plot appearance
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Statistical Power by True Population Mean",
    x = "True Population Mean",
    y = "Probability of Rejecting the Null Hypothesis"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```


The simulation results show that statistical power increases as the true population mean moves farther from the null value of zero. When the true mean is 0, the rejection rate is `r scales::percent(power_summary |> filter(true_mu == 0) |> pull(power), accuracy = 0.01)`, which is close to the nominal significance level of 5%. As the true mean increases to 2 and 3, the estimated power rises to `r scales::percent(power_summary |> filter(true_mu == 2) |> pull(power), accuracy = 0.01)` and `r scales::percent(power_summary |> filter(true_mu == 3) |> pull(power), accuracy = 0.01)`, respectively. Power approaches 100% for larger values of the true mean. These findings indicate that larger effect sizes are associated with greater statistical power when the sample size and standard deviation are held constant.

```{r}
# Compare average estimates across all simulations and rejected tests
estimate_summary =
  simulation_results |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    mean_estimate_all = mean(estimate),
    mean_estimate_rejected = mean(estimate[reject_null]),
    n_rejected = sum(reject_null),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Display the summary of estimated means
estimate_summary
```

```{r estimate_comparison_plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
# Reshape the summary data to compare the two types of estimates
estimate_plot_data =
  estimate_summary |>
  select(
    true_mu,
    mean_estimate_all,
    mean_estimate_rejected
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("mean_estimate"),
    names_to = "sample_type",
    values_to = "mean_estimate"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    sample_type = recode(
      sample_type,
      mean_estimate_all = "All Samples",
      mean_estimate_rejected = "Rejected Samples Only"
    )
  )

# Compare average estimates with the true population mean
estimate_plot_data |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = true_mu,
      y = mean_estimate,
      color = sample_type
    )
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray50"
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +

  # Customize labels and plot appearance
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "All Samples" = "steelblue",
      "Rejected Samples Only" = "coral"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimated Mean vs. True Population Mean",
    x = "True Population Mean",
    y = "Average Estimated Mean",
    color = "Simulation Samples"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```


The average estimates across all simulated samples are approximately equal to the corresponding true population means, consistent with the unbiasedness of the sample mean. However, when only samples that reject the null hypothesis are considered, the average estimates tend to exceed the true means, particularly for smaller nonzero effects. For example, when the true mean is 1, the average estimate among rejected samples is `r round(estimate_summary |> filter(true_mu == 1) |> pull(mean_estimate_rejected), 2)`, compared with `r round(estimate_summary |> filter(true_mu == 1) |> pull(mean_estimate_all), 2)` across all samples. This occurs because statistically significant results disproportionately include samples with unusually large estimated effects, introducing selection bias. As the true mean increases and statistical power approaches 100%, the difference between the two averages becomes smaller. When the true mean is zero, significant estimates can be extreme in either direction and may cancel when averaged.
